A10.text:
UN says 25 seafarers killed in, around Hormuz since US-Israel war on Iran
‘Situation cannot become new normal’, says UN’s Khaled Khiari, as Iran reports three more vessels hitting mines.
At least 25 seafarers have been killed in and around the Strait of Hormuz since the US-Israeli war on Iran broke out in February, according to the United Nations.
Khaled Khiari, assistant secretary-general for the Middle East, Asia and the Pacific, gave the figures, which cover the period up to November 11, during a UN Security Council briefing on Friday.
“This situation cannot be allowed to become the new normal,” said Khiari, urging the “full restoration of maritime navigation in the region”.
He pointed out that security incidents in and around Hormuz have been rising, with October recording the highest tally since the start of the conflict.
The UN’s International Maritime Organization (IMO) tracked 136 security incidents involving vessels in Hormuz and the wider Middle East between March 1 and November 11. It said 35 of those incidents came in October and 10 in November.
“Every day brings new reports of maritime incidents,” said Khiari. “These incidents are unacceptable,” he added. “Civilian vessels and commercial shipping must not become targets.”
His remarks come as Iranian authorities on Saturday reported that three oil tankers had hit mines while travelling through “unauthorised” or “restricted” areas of Hormuz, catching fire.
Tehran has warned vessels that they must receive Iranian approval to cross the waterway during the conflict, and has repeatedly attacked ships accused of violating its protocol.
“Any offending tanker that travels in the restricted area east of the Strait of Hormuz will be set on fire by hitting naval mines,” Iran’s navy warned in a statement carried by the country’s IRIB broadcaster.
Iranian officials have insisted the strait will not be open until the US meets its demands, which include an end to the US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, the lifting of economic sanctions, the release of Iranian frozen funds, ending fighting on all fronts, and an explicit announcement of an end to the war.
The US military claims it has cleared the strait’s main routes of mines and that the waterway is open for commercial shipping.
Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is approximately 65 percent below pre-war levels, according to the latest report from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).
Khiari, in his remarks to the UN Security Council, said “the present maritime arrangements in the Middle East remain costly, unpredictable, and unsafe”.
“Disruptions to maritime navigation continue to have significant global economic consequences, driving up energy, transport and insurance costs, fuelling inflation and threatening food security amid severely constrained fertiliser shipments.”

A115.text:
Nach tagelangen Ausfällen US-Senatoren wollen Antworten zu Starlink in der Ukraine
Auf Elon Musks Weltraumfirma SpaceX kommt offenbar eine parlamentarische Untersuchung zu: Weil SpaceX im zurückliegenden Oktober das Satelliteninternet für die Ukraine gedrosselt haben soll, muss sich das Unternehmen wohl bald den Fragen von US-Senatoren stellen.
Die Untersuchung ist eine Initiative von Senatoren der Demokraten, die im Januar die Mehrheit in der Kammer übernehmen werden. Sie verlangen von SpaceX, alle Unterlagen zu dem Thema aufzubewahren. Auch wollen sie Antworten unter anderem auf die Frage, wer die Drosselung der Geschwindigkeit für das Starlink-Internet sowie für die militärische Version Starshield angeordnet hat.
Die ukrainische Regierung hatte im Oktober tagelange Geschwindigkeitsbeschränkungen des Satelliteninternets beklagt. Damit hätten unter anderem darauf angewiesene Abwehrsysteme gegen russische Drohnen nicht eingesetzt werden können, hieß es. Diese Woche sprach der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj erneut von Einschränkungen.
SpaceX darf keine Unterlagen vernichten
Die Senatoren fordern, dass SpaceX bis zum 30. November bestätigt, keine Unterlagen zu den Vorgängen zu vernichten – und bis dahin auch ihre Fragen beantwortet. Dazu gehört etwa, welche Einschränkungen aktuell noch gelten – und die Frage, ob SpaceX mögliche Konsequenzen der Drosselung für die ukrainische Bevölkerung und Amerikaner in dem Land abgewogen habe.
Einer der Unterzeichner des Schreibens ist Chris Coons, der im Januar den Vorsitz im Außenausschuss des Senats übernehmen dürfte. Die Demokraten werden im nächsten Kongress die Mehrheit in Repräsentantenhaus und Senat halten und laufen sich bereits für Untersuchungen der Regierung von Präsident Donald Trump warm.
Die ukrainische Armee nutzt Starlink-basiertes Internet seit Beginn des russischen Angriffskriegs im Februar 2022 für ihre Kommunikation.
Europäer bei Friedensgesprächen mit am Verhandlungstisch?
Unterdessen wird weiter über mögliche Friedensgespräche diskutiert. Russland, die USA und die Ukraine sollen in jedem Fall an selbigen beteiligt sein, über die Rolle der Europäer am Verhandlungstisch herrscht teilweise noch Unklarheit.
In der Nacht zum Freitag hatten die USA signalisiert, dass der russische Präsident Wladimir Putin bereit sei, die Europäer an den Gesprächen teilnehmen zu lassen. Es gebe die Zustimmung, die europäischen Partner in die nächste Verhandlungsrunde einzubeziehen, sagte US-Unterhändler Jared Kushner.

A120.text:
Russischer Angriffskrieg Selenskyj beklagt erneute Drosselung bei Internet aus dem All
Der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj hat erneut eine Drosselung des US-Satelliteninternets Starshield über der Ukraine kritisiert. »Die Geschwindigkeitsbeschränkungen bleiben leider entlang der gesamten Frontlinie und in den vorübergehend besetzten Gebieten der Ukraine bestehen«, erklärte Selenskyj in einer Videobotschaft. Das ukrainische Außen- und das Verteidigungsministerium seien angewiesen worden, das Problem bei »allen Behörden in Amerika« anzusprechen.
»Das vorübergehend besetzte Gebiet der Ukraine gehört uns, es ist unser souveränes Hoheitsgebiet«, unterstrich der Staatschef. Die Einschränkungen seien ein »sehr schlechtes Signal« – sie beeinträchtigten die ukrainische Fähigkeit zur Drohnenabwehr. »Und ebenso gibt es Russland das Signal, dass Amerika eine andere Haltung gegenüber unseren vorübergehend besetzten Gebieten einnehmen könnte«, warnte Selenskyj. Kyjiw zähle auf eine Wiederherstellung der Geschwindigkeit.
Internetdrosselung nicht zum ersten Mal
Tags zuvor beklagte Selenskyj bereits wieder aufgetretene Beschränkungen vor allem über den russisch besetzten Teilen der Ukraine. Eine vergleichbare Drosselung gab es bereits Mitte Oktober . Elon Musk, der Eigner des Starlink-Satellitennetzwerks, warf Kyjiw dabei vor, das zivile Starlink für Drohnenangriffe eingesetzt zu haben, was gegen die Nutzungsbedingungen verstoße. Das ebenfalls von Musks Firma SpaceX bereitgestellte militärische Satelliteninternet Starshield wird hingegen von der US-Regierung kontrolliert.
Die ukrainische Armee setzt Starlink-basiertes Internet seit dem russischen Einmarsch im Februar 2022 für ihre Kommunikation ein. Mit Starlink-Terminals ausgestattete fliegende und schwimmende ukrainische Drohnen greifen ferngesteuert auch Ziele im Schwarzen Meer und in den russisch besetzten Gebieten der Ukraine an.
Kyjiws Truppen gelangen zuletzt Gebietsgewinne im Donbass, Russland stand unter Druck. Elon Musk kann das offenbar eigenhändig ändern und damit auch die Menschen weit hinter der Front gefährden .

A123.text:
Gipfel in Dublin Europäer einigen sich auf Verhandlungsteam für Gespräche mit Russland
Die Staats- und Regierungschefs der EU haben sich darauf geeinigt, wer Europa bei künftigen Gesprächen über ein Ende des Ukrainekriegs vertreten soll: Das »europäische Verhandlungsteam für den Frieden in der Ukraine« werde »aus den Institutionen der Europäischen Union und den E5« bestehen, sagte EU-Ratspräsident António Costa am Freitag nach dem informellen EU-Gipfel in Dublin. Bei den sogenannten E5-Ländern handelt es sich um Deutschland, Großbritannien, Frankreich, Italien und Polen.
Bei den EU-Institutionen handele es sich um die EU-Kommission und den Rat der EU-Länder, erläuterte Kommissionspräsidentin Ursula von der Leyen. »Wir werden die Ukraine unterstützen und unsere Interessen schützen«, betonte sie. Die Bundesregierung begrüßte die Entscheidung. Sie sehe sich »in ihrer bisherigen Verhandlungspraxis bestätigt«, teilte ein Regierungssprecher mit. Nun sei es »wichtig, sich auf die Inhalte einer Friedenslösung zu konzentrieren«.
Costa sagte, die Grundsätze und die Position der EU in den Verhandlungen seien bekannt, »und unser europäisches Team wird weiterhin in enger Abstimmung und in vollkommener Geschlossenheit handeln«. Europa müsse »in allen Gesprächen, die die Zukunft der Ukraine und die Sicherheit unseres Kontinents prägen, mit einer klaren und geeinten Stimme sprechen«, mahnte er. Die EU spiele »eine zentrale Rolle bei den Gesprächen über die europäische Zukunft der Ukraine, ihren Wiederaufbau und ihren Wohlstand«.
Wer Europa auf höchster Ebene vertritt, bleibt unklar
Die Einigung ist ein Kompromiss zwischen unterschiedlichen Interessen: Mehrere kleine EU-Staaten hatten sich dafür ausgesprochen, dass offizielle Vertreter der EU-Spitze mögliche Gespräche mit Russland führen sollten. Der estnische Ministerpräsident Kristen Michal sagte, bei Friedensgesprächen sollten der portugiesische EU-Ratspräsident António Costa und die aus seinem Heimatland stammende EU-Außenbeauftragte Kaja Kallas für die EU sprechen. Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz machte hingegen klar, dass er fest mit einer direkten Beteiligung Deutschlands an den Friedensgesprächen rechne. »Es soll erstmals in den nächsten Wochen jetzt konkrete Friedensgespräche geben, in denen Europa vertreten ist«, sagte Merz in Dublin. »Deutschland ist dabei gesetzt, das ist völlig klar.«
Weiterhin ungeklärt ist allerdings, wer die europäische Seite bei eventuellen Gesprächen auf höchster Ebene mit US-Präsident Donald Trump, Kremlchef Wladimir Putin und dem ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj vertreten würde.
Die Diskussion darüber, wer für Europa am Verhandlungstisch sitzen soll, hatte angesichts der von den USA vermittelten Gespräche zwischen der Ukraine und Russland zuletzt an Fahrt aufgenommen. Nach Gesprächen mit dem russischen Präsidenten Wladimir Putin hatte der US-Sondergesandte Steve Witkoff angekündigt, am nächsten Verhandlungstermin der USA, Russlands und der Ukraine solle auch Europa teilnehmen. »Die Europäer werden beim nächsten Treffen dabei sein, was wir für eine sehr große Sache halten, denn es ist wichtig – sie sind unsere Partner, und es ist wichtig, dass sie einbezogen werden«, sagte Witkoff gegenüber Reportern.

A16.text:
Ukraine is running out of options, and Russia knows it
As Russian strikes push Kyiv towards compromise, Western governments are beginning to reconsider the security demands Moscow has made for years.
The trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the United States that took place in Abu Dhabi this week may not lead to a rapid breakthrough, but they clearly outline the trajectory of a conflict that might, after all, be nearing its end.
If anything illustrates the political and emotional rift the two sides are yet to bridge, it is President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s remarks in Copenhagen this week, in which he lamented that Russian leader Vladimir Putin was still alive. Ukraine’s harsh reality, however, is pushing him towards an unsavoury compromise with his arch-enemy.
Kyiv was compelled to enter the talks at the most disadvantageous moment, when it has few means to counter devastating Russian air strikes that damage its key industries and cripple essential infrastructure in major cities. One of Ukraine’s top negotiators, David Arakhamia, who leads Zelenskyy’s parliamentary faction, described the negotiations as among the most difficult he had participated in since 2022. He said the Russians had arrived with very strict instructions and that it had been difficult to soften the tone of the discussions. His assessment confirms that Russia sees itself as well equipped to negotiate from a position of force.
Moscow, meanwhile, expressed optimism about the outcome. Putin’s aide, Vladimir Medinsky, said the talks had brought the two countries closer to peace. Even Arakhamia said there was momentum towards reaching a solution before the end of the year. That optimism, it needs to be noted, comes without any signs of Russia changing its position on the contours of the agreement. Just as it has for years, the Kremlin insists on a genuinely neutral, demilitarised Ukraine which honours the rights of its Russian-speaking population.
If all this comes as a nasty surprise to many in the West, that’s because for most of this year, Western politicians and the mainstream media kept insisting that the tide of war was turning and that Ukraine was getting the upper hand. Their optimism was fuelled by Ukrainian long-range strikes targeting Russian oil refineries as well as by the snail’s pace of Russian advances on the battlefield.
As late as September, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said that “in all but name, Russia has already lost the war”. Around the same time, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said Russia was not doing well in Ukraine.
When NATO leaders convened for the Ankara summit in July, it seemed that even US President Donald Trump had bought into the idea that Ukraine had the battlefield advantage.
But Russia responded to Ukraine’s surge, backed up by European funds and US intelligence-sharing, with round-the-clock air strikes that are bringing Ukraine close to its pain barrier. Moscow’s message was cruel: any damage Ukraine and the West might inflict on Russia would be met with epic devastation in Ukraine, from which it would take decades to recover.
The coming winter spells nationwide humanitarian disaster. Russian strikes on energy infrastructure have disrupted electricity and central heating supplies. Millions of Ukrainians, particularly in major cities, live in apartment blocks dependent on central heating, without which their homes can become virtually unliveable. Generators can provide temporary power, but their use is making the cost of war enormous for Ukraine and Western taxpayers who fund its war effort.
It is these dire circumstances, rather than pressure from Trump’s administration, that have forced Ukraine to enter the talks. Zelenskyy would have waited at least until the spring had he not felt so pressed.
Ukraine’s surge has failed to shift Moscow’s peace conditions one inch. Meanwhile, the Western perception of this war’s realities has undergone a considerable transformation.
[truncated]

A177.text:
France among five major powers to represent EU in Ukraine talks
European Council President Antonio Costa on Friday said that Brussels will send diplomats from the bloc and five countries, including the UK, France, Germany, Italy and Poland, to upcoming Ukraine talks.
Europe will send a team of diplomats from the European Union and five individual countries to the next round of Ukraine talks, a top EU official said Friday, following a summit focused on how to avoid being shut out of US-led negotiations on ending the nearly five-year war.
European Council President Antonio Costa said the continent will be represented by officials from the 27-nation EU bloc and five members of the “Coalition of the Willing” that backs Ukraine: the UK, France, Germany, Italy and Poland.
“We need to integrate all of us. And for this it's essential to have a team and to speak with only one voice,” Costa said.
European leaders have been concerned that a US-backed process will leave them sidelined and Kyiv vulnerable as Moscow and Washington decide the fate of a conflict that has roiled the continent.
Ukraine is eager for support from its European allies. It's reluctant to leave the talks solely in the hands of a US administration that has often seemed to lean toward Moscow’s views. Russia, for its part, does not want European countries involved in direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine’s military effort.
European leaders also distrust US President Donald Trump to negotiate on their behalf after a series of tense standoffs over trade, Greenland and conflicts in Iran and Ukraine.
“Without Europeans, there is no support for Ukraine,” French President Emmanuel Macron said Thursday at a meeting of the European Political Community in Dublin. “There is no more US support.”
“At the end of the day, we will be the ones to define and decide for our future security as Europeans,” he said.
'They will have a voice'
European leaders fear Russian President Vladimir Putin will press Trump to back a peace settlement that weakens not just Ukraine but broader European security. Putin has demanded NATO troops be pulled back from Russia’s borders and that no European forces be deployed in Ukraine.
As envoys from Washington, Moscow and Kyiv met this week in Abu Dhabi, several European countries, including the UK, France and Germany, attended discussions nearby, but not the main talks.
Read moreAbu Dhabi peace talks show US, Europe and Ukraine are ‘aligned’, NATO chief says
US envoy Jared Kushner and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said after they met in Dublin late Thursday that Europe would be part of the next round of talks. Zelensky said Europe would send a negotiating team, adding that “they will have a voice".
“We cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table,” Kushner said, adding that Putin was “willing to give it a try.”
United but not unified
European leaders are united in wanting a place at the table. But they have tussled over whether Europe should be represented by one person — as Russia has demanded and the US suggested it would prefer — or a team, ultimately opting for the latter.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that “the Europeans squabble like spiders in a jar” and that they should name a representative.
Supporters of a single envoy, such as Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, argued that the absence of a united European voice has allowed individual countries or small groups to engage in freelance diplomacy.
“There are too many different groupings discussing the issue,” she said.
The question of who represents Europe is an old one. Europe itself is loosely defined. Is it the 27-nation EU, the 32-nation NATO military alliance made up mostly of European countries, the 29-nation Schengen zone, or the 47-nation European Political Community?
That has long frustrated Washington.
[truncated]

A196.text:
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Friday called for an “immediate and drastic reduction” in greenhouse gas emissions, as divisions over fossil fuels dominated the first week of COP31 climate talks in Turkey.
Big fossil fuel producers and consumers at the talks are resisting any deal that would specify firm new targets or a shift away from oil, gas and coal, observers said as the first week of talks drew to a close.
That poses a challenge for summit host Turkey and lead negotiator Australia, which have another week to land the kind of ambitious agreement climate advocates such as Guterres say is needed.
“The central question is in the hands of member states, particularly the big emitters. They must recognize the need for an immediate and drastic reduction in emissions to keep the 1.5 goal still possible by the end of the century,” he said, referring to the warming limit countries had agreed to pursue under the 2015 Paris Agreement.
A UN report last month found the world is on course to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius warming threshold, a limit scientists say should prevent the worst effects of climate change.
As temperatures have risen, this year has been marked by extreme heatwaves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a flood that killed more than 1,450 people. Thousands more are still missing.
Major oil producers such as Saudi Arabia and Russia have traditionally resisted language constraining fossil fuels, while large developing economies such as India have opposed measures they say could limit their development and energy choices, a dynamic that has compromised the outcomes of past deals.
World leaders set out clashing priorities at COP31 leaving negotiators with an uphill battle
The world’s biggest oil consumer, the United States, meanwhile, has skipped the talks for the second year in a row under President Donald Trump, who has called global warming a hoax and promoted continued use of fossil fuels.
“We must confront the disproportionate influence of the fossil fuel lobby. The future of our planet cannot be negotiated on the terms of those profiting from its destruction,” said Guterres, who is leaving his job at the end of December after two five-year terms.
“But I remain hopeful. I’ve also seen something extraordinary over these 10 years. Renewable energy has moved from the margins to the mainstream. The economics have changed. The technology has advanced. A cleaner, safer, and more secure energy future is in our hands. The question is whether we have the courage and speed to reach for it.”
COP31 host Turkey is striving to place a proposal to expand global electrification at the centre of an eventual deal, saying the plan will lead to emissions cuts by speeding the shift away from fossil fuel-powered cars, boilers and other equipment.
The proposal does not require the increased electricity use to come from renewable sources, although some countries, including last year’s COP host Brazil, are advocating for progress on a plan to require countries to more clearly map out their transition away from fossil fuels.
Katrine Petersen, an observer for the non-governmental organization E3G, said whether those measures survive the talks depends on conversations in the days to come.
“We’ve also heard quite clearly from countries like India, the G77, that they don’t want any firm targets. They don’t want any kind of technology or fuel-specific language,” she said. “[These are] the kind of consistent and ongoing divides that we’ve seen from those different parties before.”
UN sees higher global warming even if countries reduce heat-trapping emissions
Representatives from India, Saudi Arabia and Russia did not immediately comment.
Diana Acconcia, head of the EU delegation, said Europe backed the electrification goal.
“Electrification is, in a way, an inclusive agenda because it is nonprescriptive in a way on how the electrification is achieved,” she said.
[truncated]

Ukrainian drones knock out 36% of Russia's oil refining capacity in under two weeks
Smoke is rising in Leningrad Oblast after the drone attack, Nov. 11, 2026 (Photo: Social Media/via REUTERS)
Ukrainian drone strikes knocked out 36% of Russia’s total oil refining capacity in less than two weeks, hitting at least nine major refineries between Oct. 30 and Nov. 11, defense manufacturer Fire Point reported on Nov. 12.
The combined annual processing capacity of the Russian plants hit over the past 13 days exceeds 120 million metric tons of crude oil—accounting for 36% of the aggressor state’s entire domestic oil refining capacity.
"In under two weeks, enterprises accounting for more than a third of Russia's total oil refining capacity came under strike," Fire Point noted.
Recent Strikes on Russian Refineries
On Nov. 6, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that in direct retaliation for Russian strikes against Ukraine’s energy grid, Kyiv would press forward with its campaign targeting the aggressor state's oil refining infrastructure.
On Nov. 7, long-range drones struck Saratov Oil Refinery. Two days later, on Nov. 9, Ukrainian forces hit Russia's second-largest processing facility — Kirishi Oil Refinery in Leningrad Oblast.
On Nov. 11, strike drones hit oil export terminals at the Baltic port of Ust-Luga, a vital maritime hub for Russian crude shipments.
According to Reuters, Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries since late October 2026 have reduced Russia's operational refining capacity by roughly 30% and triggered acute fuel shortages across at least six Russian oblasts.

A24.text:
Trump, Xi and Putin to hold first three-way summit in China
White House says Trump plans to discuss the Iran war and nuclear arms at a meeting on the sidelines of APEC next week.
Leaders of the United States, China and Russia are set to hold an unprecedented three-way meeting next week, the White House has said.
US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China’s tech hub, the White House assistant press secretary confirmed in an announcement.
The talks will be held nine months after the last nuclear arms treaty between Washington and Moscow expired, leaving the world’s two countries with the largest atomic arsenals without caps for the first time in more than 50 years.
What’s on the agenda?
Trump has said the meeting is a chance for all three countries to reach a deal on nuclear stockpiles.
The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) lapsed in February. Trump then rejected Russia’s proposal to extend it for another year and demanded a “new, improved and modernised” deal that includes China.
Expectations are low. “We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior Trump administration official told the Reuters news agency, describing the meeting as the start of a conversation.
Russia holds the most nuclear warheads, followed by the US, then China, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
Trump plans on discussing the Iran war with Xi and Putin, but will steer away from discussing Russia’s war in Ukraine, according to a senior US official who briefed reporters on condition of anonymity.
Elon Musk will also travel with Trump to China but will not attend the meeting, the official added. Trump is also not expected to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during the Asia trip.
Yalta Conference comparisons
The planned summit has drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the leaders of the US, Britain and the Soviet Union shaped the post-war order.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, however, dismissed the parallel, saying any agreements reached in Shenzhen cannot be imposed on others, but he still called the meeting “extremely significant”.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has voiced concern that the meeting could become a platform to discuss a Ukraine deal behind Kyiv’s back.
Trump has pursued closer ties with both leaders despite a short-lived trade war with China last year and Russia’s continuing war in Ukraine, where Washington is seeking to mediate a solution.

A28.text:
Trump to raise nuclear-arms cuts with Putin, Xi on Thursday, White House says
By Trevor Hunnicutt and Jasper Ward
WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump will raise nuclear-arms reduction at a meeting in China next week with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President XiJinping, the White House said on Friday.
"He will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, said on a call with reporters. She added that the meeting would take place on Thursday in China.
Trump's repeated insistence that the first-of-its-kind meeting of the three leaders focus on nuclear arms reductions has riled China, which is hosting a summit focused on trade and commerce. China has rebuffed attempts to talk about nuclear arms with Russia and the United States, which have the largest stockpiles of such weapons.
Putin, Xi and Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen. Trump is leaving on Monday for a four-day trip to Asia that also includes a stop in the Philippines.
"We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement," a senior Trump administration official said regarding the nuclear issue. "This is a difficult topic for China to address, but we do think it's time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults' table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things."
The official added: "This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward."
Beijing has for years resisted direct engagement with Washington about its nuclear program, saying it is more appropriate for Russia and the US to speak directly because of their large arsenals.
Russia has the most stored nuclear warheads, followed by the United States and China, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty between the US and Russiaexpired this year.
It was not clear whether Russia or China intended to engage in a conversation about arms reductions with Trump.
The Chinese and Russian embassies in Washington did not immediately respond to emailed requests for comment.
Trump will also raise the US-Israeli war against Iran in the meeting but is not expected to raise Russia's war in Ukraine, the official said.
The Republican president is not expected to have a one-on-one meeting with Putin or discuss Ukraine's access to satellite communications service provided by Elon Musk's SpaceX. Musk is joining Trump on the trip to China but will not attend his meeting with Xi and Putin, according to the official.
"We've had many meetings recently with the Russians, but China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there," the person said.
Trump is also not expected to meet with North Korean leader Kim JongUn during his trip to Asia, according to the official.
(Reporting by Jasper Ward and Trevor Hunnicutt in Washington; Editing by Caitlin Webber)

A38.text:
UN chief urges drastic emissions cuts as COP31 wrestles with fossil fuels
ANTALYA, Turkey, Nov 13 (Reuters) - UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Friday called for an "immediate and drastic reduction" in greenhouse gas emissions, as divisions over fossil fuels dominated the first week of COP31 climate talks in Turkey.
Big fossil fuel producers and consumers at the talks are resisting any deal that would specify firm new targets or a shift away from oil, gas and coal, observers said as the first week of talks drew to a close.
That poses a challenge for summit host Turkey and lead negotiator Australia, which have another week to land the kind of ambitious agreement climate advocates such as Guterres say is needed.
"The central question is in the hands of member states, particularly the big emitters. They must recognise the need for an immediate and drastic reduction in emissions to keep the 1.5 goal still possible by the end of the century," he said, referring to the warming limit countries had agreed to pursue under the 2015 Paris Agreement.
A UN report last month found the world is on course to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warming threshold, a limit scientists say should prevent the worst effects of climate change.
As temperatures have risen, this year has been marked by extreme heatwaves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a flood that killed more than 1,450 people. Thousands more are still missing.
THE FOSSIL FUEL LOBBY
Major oil producers such as Saudi Arabia and Russia have traditionally resisted language constraining fossil fuels, while large developing economies such as India have opposed measures they say could limit their development and energy choices, a dynamic that has compromised the outcomes of past deals.
The world’s biggest oil consumer, the United States, meanwhile, has skipped the talks for the second year in a row under President Donald Trump, who has called global warming a hoax and promoted continued use of fossil fuels.
"We must confront the disproportionate influence of the fossil fuel lobby. The future of our planet cannot be negotiated on the terms of those profiting from its destruction," said Guterres, who is leaving his job at the end of December after two five-year terms.
"But I remain hopeful. I've also seen something extraordinary over these 10 years. Renewable energy has moved from the margins to the mainstream. The economics have changed. The technology has advanced. A cleaner, safer, and more secure energy future is in our hands. The question is whether we have the courage and speed to reach for it."
ELECTRIFICATION AND NO FIRM TARGETS
COP31 host Turkey is striving to place a proposal to expand global electrification at the centre of an eventual deal, saying the plan will lead to emissions cuts by speeding the shift away from fossil fuel-powered cars, boilers and other equipment.
The proposal does not require the increased electricity use to come from renewable sources, although some countries, including last year’s COP host Brazil, are advocating for progress on a plan to require countries to more clearly map out their transition away from fossil fuels.
Katrine Petersen, an observer for the non-governmental organisation E3G, said whether those measures survive the talks depends on conversations in the days to come.
"We've also heard quite clearly from countries like India, the G77, that they don't want any firm targets. They don't want any kind of technology or fuel-specific language," she said. "(These are) the kind of consistent and ongoing divides that we've seen from those different parties before."
Representatives from India, Saudi Arabia and Russia did not immediately comment.
Diana Acconcia, head of the EU delegation, said Europe backed the electrification goal.
"Electrification is, in a way, an inclusive agenda because it is non-prescriptive in a way on how the electrification is achieved," she said.

A48.text:
A global outage taking down a wide range of Microsoft 365 services remains ongoing Friday morning.
The outage started midday Thursday, impacting users of Microsoft email, cloud, and AI services. Microsoft has documented the full list of services impacted by the error, while moving early Friday morning to protect customers around the world from losing emails during the extended disruptions.
“Recovery actions are ongoing,” the Microsoft 365 Status account confirmed on X. “To help preserve delayed mail during this event, we’ve extended email timeout to 48 hours.”
Similar to recent world-shaking outages of widely used tech like Amazon Web Services and CrowdStrike, the Microsoft disruption looks like “one of the biggest outages of all time,” Ciaran Martin, the former head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, told NBC News. Possibly even “worse,” he suggested.
Businesses, hospitals, police departments, and schools were among those scrambling to work around the outage. In Japan, it disrupted government IT infrastructure, according to deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki. NBC’s report documented various harms, noting that “few public bodies were immune from the outage.” In some cases, doctors couldn’t send patients “important” updates on medication changes or follow-up care.
The financial sector suffered, too, with people blocked from making bank transfers since they couldn’t receive verification codes.
Justice systems were also hobbled. The Supreme Court in the Philippines saw its legal work derailed, NBC reported. And one US sheriff’s office in Colorado reported that the outage made it difficult for people to post bond for prisoners’ immediate release.
It’s unclear how many users were affected, but Microsoft estimated in January that the total number of paid Microsoft 365 commercial subscriptions exceeded 450 million.
Microsoft blames failed server health checks
On a status page, Microsoft said “we have no evidence of malicious activity associated with this incident” and promised to “share a full Post-Incident Report with root cause and defense-in-depth actions after mitigation is complete.”
“We’re aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact,” Microsoft said on X.
But Microsoft’s public statements make clear that the tech giant was blindsided by the outage and struggled for hours to find mitigations that could reliably restore user access.

A5.text:
Qatar and Turkiye sign a mutual defence pact: What do we know?
Analysts say the pact, agreed amid the US-Iran war, aims to deter attacks rather than build an offensive alliance.
Qatar and Turkiye have welcomed a new mutual defence agreement that commits them to a common position against any external armed attack on either country.
The pact followed Friday’s high-level meeting of the Turkiye-Qatar Supreme Strategic Committee in Istanbul, chaired by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.
It comes as the region deals with the fallout of the United States-Israeli war on Iran and disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
So what is in the agreement, and why does it matter now? Here’s what you need to know:
What does the agreement say?
According to a joint communique, the deal aims to strengthen collective defence, promote regional security and establish a common position against external armed attacks targeting either or both countries.
It reflects “not only the commitment of its signatories to safeguarding their sovereignty and territorial integrity, but also their shared vision of contributing to a more secure and stable regional order”, the statement said.
The two countries agreed to consult one another on security threats and defence policy. They also agreed to expand joint military exercises, defence industry collaboration and personnel training exchanges.
The communique, as reported, did not set out what could trigger the agreement or what form a joint response would take.
Other agreements reached at the meeting covered education, consumer protection, and peace, reconciliation and conflict resolution, Qatar’s Al Raya newspaper said in an editorial on Saturday.
Is this a military alliance?
Not an offensive one, analysts say.
Abdulla Banndar Al-Etaibi, an assistant professor in the Department of International Affairs at Qatar University, told Al Jazeera that the goal is not to form an alliance against any particular country.
Instead, he said, it is meant to raise the cost of any potential aggression so that others are deterred from attempting it.
He said cooperation already rests on an extended military partnership, including a Turkish military presence, joint training and defence manufacturing.
The partnership is moving to a more advanced level, based on converging security doctrines and a shared view of where threats come from and how to deal with them, said Al-Etaibi.
Why is the timing important?
The region is braced for more conflict.
There are fears of a renewed military escalation, pushing states to build up their defences and deterrence, Al-Etaibi said.
The deal comes amid Israel’s aggressive military posture and growing questions over the future reliability of the US security umbrella.
Regional states are looking to new alliances built on deterrence, joint arms manufacturing and less dependence on outside powers.
In the communique, Ankara and Doha said the war on Iran and its regional repercussions must be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy.
They called for “the swift and full resumption of safe, secure and unimpeded passage through the Strait of Hormuz”.
Why does defence manufacturing matter?
Because supply chains have become a weak point.
Al-Etaibi said disruption to navigation in Hormuz has made it harder to rely on foreign military supply chains.
Producing weapons locally and securing spare parts is now a strategic necessity, not just an economic choice, he said.
Mahjoob Zweiri, an academic and Middle East policy expert, told Al Jazeera that the move to joint manufacturing marks an advanced strategic stage.
Military industries require billions of dollars of investment and long-term commitments, he said, as well as mutual trust over technology transfer. He said the war had shown why countries need their own manufacturing capacity, pointing to Iran, which kept fighting by producing much of its weaponry at home.
[truncated]

Pressure grows on Trump's Commerce Secretary Lutnick in fallout from Nvidia scandal
- Published
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips, as the fallout from the Nvidia scandal widens to President Donald Trump's cabinet.
Pressure is building on Lutnick from across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions.
Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy.
Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but was not on a list of firms US companies are prevented from working with.
Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".
"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.
Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.
Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China.
"President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.
Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment.
There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but the Financial Times separately reported that the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included.
However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia.
"The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC, external.

"It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."
Bessent's pointed comments are a rare instance of internal debate within the Trump administration spilling out into the public view, although tensions have reportedly simmered between Bessent and Lutnick in the past.
In 2024, the two reportedly jostled for the role of treasury secretary ahead of Trump's return to the White House, and last year the pair butted heads over the administration's tariff policy, according to US media.

A63.text:
German spies handed new powers to tackle 'hybrid threats' from abroad
- Published
Germany's foreign and domestic intelligence services are to be given greater powers to combat espionage, terrorism and sabotage after the country's parliament, the Bundestag, approved a major overhaul of its legislation.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, who championed the bill, has called it a "reform of the century", necessary because of the increasing threats from foreign powers.
But the Left Party's security spokeswoman, Clara Bünger, said Dobrindt was creating a new German secret police.
The legislation gives numerous new powers to Germany's BND federal intelligence service, and its BfV domestic service, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution.
In the Bundestag, 309 MPs voted in favour of the new law on intelligence services, while 190 voted against and 71 abstained.
For historical reasons, German intelligence has mainly focused on gathering information rather than acting on it.
In future, German spies working for the BND, which is responsible for foreign intelligence, will be able to conduct covert operations abroad, including sabotage.
This could include paralysing the servers of state-sponsored hacker groups, disrupting disinformation networks, or even disrupting supply chains for weapons.
Agents for the domestic intelligence service, the BfV, will no longer to be limited to gathering information. For the first time they will be able to take protective action against property and IT systems, if specific threats are identified.
That means they will be allowed to dismantle or break explosives or weapons, divert or block data flows during cyber-attacks, delete or falsify data stored for malicious purposes, and plant false information on those involved.
- Sabotage suspect held in Germany after spate of attacks on power grid 
  - Published8 September
- Germany says Russia behind Leipzig airport drone attack 
  - Published2 September
Under certain conditions, BfV agents will also be permitted to enter homes covertly. However, the measure must always be authorised in advance.
They will also be given wider powers of digital surveillance, including monitoring encrypted telecommunications and carrying out online searches. They will also be allowed to use AI-supported data analysis and biometric image matching on the internet.
The government says the reform is needed because of an increase in foreign espionage, particularly from Russia, China and Iran.
"We are the target of hybrid threats," said Dobrindt. "Germany is a theatre of operations for terrorism, extremism and foreign powers."
In August, a drone carrying an explosive device was discovered at Leipzig Airport, close to Ukrainian cargo planes. However, it failed to explode as the bomb's detonator was apparently faulty.
German authorities say Russia was behind the attack.
The new law has been bitterly criticised by some opposition politicians, even though Dobrindt has said it is "madness" to think it means that Germany is creating a new secret police.
And Clara Bünger from the Left Party told public broadcaster ARD that the new law was "a monster… summoning ghosts that we will probably never be able to get rid of".
The separation between the police and the secret service, she warned, was "being eroded" - and Bünger said that had been a lesson learned from the Nazi era.
"This means the secret service is being granted executive powers and will not only be allowed to act pre-emptively, but will also be granted police powers."
However, Sonja Eichwede of the centre-left SPD, which is part of Germany's governing coalition, said the reforms would make a significant contribution to ensuring the country's democracy was "robust and resilient".

A72.text:
How the Jensen Huang scandal created a headache for business-friendly Singapore
- Published
A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.
On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips.
For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets.
With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years.
Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns.
But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.
Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips.
Megaspeed is a case in point.
It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.
The city-state has had some success in policing this.
It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places.
They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties.
In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore.
The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere.
Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed.
But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department.
Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud.
In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months.
Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case.
Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing.
In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times.
[truncated]

A79.text:
World
Microsoft reports progress in reviving some services amid global outage disrupting businesses, governments
Outage highlights overreliance on small group of global tech firms, experts say
Microsoft said progress is being made in bringing its popular workplace software back online as a global outage enters its second day, disrupting business communications, police crime reporting, court operations, AI tools and many other services.
The company said server issues were behind the incident that also affected its Copilot AI assistant and that a broader rollout of software fixes was starting to stabilize the system. It said it was not aware of any malicious activity.
The Redmond, Wash.-based company said it was trying different ways to identify the cause of the problem and get its servers back online, using "a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure."
Microsoft said in a new update that it was seeing "broader improvements" in North America and much of Europe.
- No timeline for when Microsoft's multi-day outage might be fully fixed, company says
- How Microsoft's global outage is affecting some Montreal services
Outlook and Teams are two of the most widely used workplace applications, with hundreds of millions of users. The outage prevented people from performing essential functions such as sending emails, managing calendars and hosting virtual meetings.
It affected government agencies from Australia to Japan to the United States, caused delays at trading firms, hindered some companies from publishing earnings and prompted airlines to warn customers of communication lags, according to public statements.
The outage is one of the longest in Microsoft's history and the second disruption to its services this year.
Questions about tech reliance, cloud systems
Organizations that host Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than in the cloud, were somewhat spared.
Microsoft said the outage specifically hit features tied to Exchange Online — its cloud-based email and scheduling hub — leaving unconnected applications operational.
The incident deepens questions about the global reliance on a handful of Big Tech companies that supply both the essential software and the cloud infrastructure that underpins it.
Microsoft shares were down 0.4 per cent in early trading. They have gained roughly 8 per cent so far this year.
Disruptions and financial losses from the outage could result in numerous insurance claims, but the overall hit to insurers is expected to be limited, said Mario De Cicco, vice-president of European financial institutions at Morningstar DBRS.
De Cicco estimated global insured losses from the incident at between $300 million US and $500 million US, well below the $400 million US to $1.5 billion US financial toll from the 2024 CrowdStrike outage that crashed more than eight million Windows-based computers and caused widespread disruptions.
Caitlin Egen of Control Risks said that big global firms usually have contingency plans, but when key services went down abruptly it was still a "wake-up call."
"For a lot of businesses this morning, it's probably been chaos trying to figure out how to even get in touch with people," she said.
Hospitals, trains grapple with outage
European exchange operator Euronext, which runs exchanges in Paris, Brussels, Lisbon, Amsterdam, Oslo, Athens and Milan, told listed companies to pick up the phone.
Aviva, which reported earnings on Friday, said it had put backup plans in place, including sending out alternative phone numbers for earnings calls and using Bluetooth to transfer recordings because email was down.
Unity Health Toronto said its teams are experiencing difficulties sending and receiving emails, but that patient and resident care is not affected by the outage.
In Montreal, the CHUM hospital said the outage affected appointment requests and some internal activities.
[truncated]

A80.text:
World
U.S. Treasury Secretary frustrated by Commerce Department's inaction on Nvidia chips
Bessent supports adding Megaspeed International to export control list
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday he was frustrated with the U.S. Commerce Department's delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to a company led by an alleged Chinese spy.
Bessent said on CNBC that his department, along with the U.S. departments of State and Defence and the U.S. trade representative, were in favour of adding Singapore-based Megaspeed International to an export control list for months but that the Commerce Department was in charge of the matter.
"Commerce has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent said. "My deputy has been pushing this for months."
Bessent's comments were an unusually public rebuke of a fellow cabinet member, in this case U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Commerce oversees U.S. government controls over exports of sensitive, high-tech goods.
The comments come as Nvidia's ties to Megaspeed play a prominent role in the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Huang allegedly had an affair with the CEO of Megaspeed, Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence suspects is a Chinese spy, the New York Times has reported. China has denied allegations of spying.
Lutnick has come under increasing scrutiny because of his reportedly close relationship with Jensen Huang. The ex-Nvidia CEO is also close to U.S. President Donald Trump and visited the White House on Sept. 29 to discuss AI safety.
- What the Jensen Huang scandal means for Trump and his administration
- The Nvidia scandal has wiped away $1T in value. What that means for your investments
The Times reported Thursday that Lutnick resisted placing greater limits on the sale of Nvidia's more advanced chips to China. Chinese firms have accessed Nvidia's chips through companies like Megaspeed, which has reportedly purchased more than $4 billion US worth of Nvidia's advanced semiconductors.
The split in Trump's cabinet reflects the widespread fallout from the scandal that has engulfed Nvidia, one of the most valuable publicly traded companies in the world. Nvidia's computer chips play a central role in the buildout of artificial intelligence, powering AI models such as those developed by OpenAI and Anthropic.
U.S. interest in restricting chip sales
The U.S. government has, since the Biden administration, sought to restrict the sale of the most advanced AI computer chips to China in an effort to protect U.S. technology companies' lead. Yet China has at times retaliated, creating controversy over how far the U.S. should push its restrictions.
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment.
Bessent declined to comment Friday on the Times report that he confronted Lutnick last week in the White House's situation room about Megaspeed.
Separately, Axios reported this week that Lutnick received a classified memo this spring warning about Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected spy.
- Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after affair raises national security concerns
- How China gets around the U.S. ban on Nvidia chips
Last year, Megaspeed was accused of illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December the company said there was "no evidence" of such exports.
The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security began investigating Megaspeed International in 2024. The bureau later handed off the investigation to the U.S. Justice Department.
A person familiar with the bureau's investigation denied any intervention from Nvidia. The person wasn't authorized to discuss the matter publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.
[truncated]

A84.text:
World
UN nuclear watchdog increasingly concerned about Iranian enrichment plant, report says
Iran told IAEA that nuclear monitoring talks cannot proceed while under threat from military attacks
The United Nations nuclear watchdog is "increasingly concerned" about a uranium-enrichment plant at Isfahan that Iran declared to it last year but has still not let the watchdog inspect, it said in a confidential report on Iran on Friday seen by Reuters and The Associated Press.
Iran has not let International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors return to any of its nuclear facilities bombed by Israel and the United States in a 12-day campaign in June last year that destroyed or badly damaged Iran's other uranium enrichment plants, the heart of its nuclear program.
The targets included a tunnel network at Isfahan where diplomats have said they believe the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant (IFEP) — declared to the agency on June 12, 2025 — is located, though a senior diplomat said that its whereabouts and status remained unknown.
The IAEA had planned to inspect the plant on June 13, 2025, but the bombing campaign started that day, making it impossible.
"The agency does not know IFEP's exact location, status for safeguards purposes or whether it contains nuclear material," the confidential IAEA report to member states said, adding that "the agency is also increasingly concerned that Iran has not permitted" it to inspect the plant or see design plans.
Iran said the situation won't resolve "until the root causes of the present situation are addressed and the essential requirements for normal safeguards implementation are restored," the report added.
- Canada reimposes sanctions on Iran for violating nuclear non-proliferation commitments
- Analysis North Korea expands its nuclear arsenal after witnessing Iran’s vulnerability
IAEA chief Rafael Grossi said in March his agency believed a significant amount of Iran's most highly enriched uranium was in the tunnel complex at Isfahan.
While the report singled out IFEP, it also reiterated that Iran should inform the IAEA of the status of its enrichment plants, as well as its stock of highly enriched uranium, which includes material close to weapons grade, and let inspectors return to the bombed sites and account for the enriched uranium.
"The agency's lack of information about this nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of serious proliferation concern … and needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency," it said.
Iran also expressed concern in a letter to the IAEA about a recent U.S. offer of a reward of up to $20 million US in exchange for information on Iran's nuclear program. Tehran stressed the importance of maintaining the "confidentiality" of the IAEA's activities and the need to ensure that information on Iran's nuclear program is not "disclosed, misused or exploited."
The IAEA encouraged Iran to "consider technical and gradual measures" to allow for a return of inspectors to Iran.
The only facility inspected in Iran by the IAEA since last June is the Bushehr nuclear power plant. Inspectors conducted an inspection there on Sept. 12-15. The reactor currently running at Bushehr uses uranium from Russia enriched to 4.5 per cent — a low level needed for power generation in such plants.
The U.S. and Israel launched further military strikes against Iran on Feb. 28 with attacks that killed Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other top officials. The strikes targeted Revolutionary Guard command facilities, air defence systems, missile and drone launch sites, and military airfields.
According to the IAEA , Iran maintains a stockpile of 440.9 kilograms of uranium enriched up to 60 per cent purity — a short, technical step away from weapons-grade levels of 90 per cent.
That stockpile could allow Iran to build as many as 10 nuclear bombs, should it decide to weaponize its program, Grossi warned in an interview with The Associated Press last year.

A121.text:
Dreiergespräch geplant Trump trifft Putin und Xi kommende Woche in China
US-Präsident Donald Trump trifft nach Angaben des Weißen Hauses in der kommenden Woche zu Gesprächen mit Russlands Präsident Wladimir Putin und Chinas Staatschef Xi Jinping zusammen. Das trilaterale Treffen werde kommende Woche Donnerstag am Rande des Gipfels der Asiatisch-Pazifischen Wirtschaftsgemeinschaft (Apec) im chinesischen Shenzhen stattfinden, teilte das Weiße Haus am Freitag mit.
»Der Präsident hat deutlich gemacht, dass er unter anderem den Abbau von Atomwaffen weltweit erörtern wird«, sagte die Sprecherin des Weißen Hauses, Olivia Wales, vor Journalisten.
Laut einem ranghohen US-Regierungsvertreter wird es bei den Gesprächen zwischen Trump und seinen Kollegen aus China und Russland auch den Krieg in Iran gehen. Es sei jedoch nicht davon auszugehen, dass Trump auf den Ukrainekrieg eingehen werde, sagte der Beamte am Freitag.
»Ich denke, der Präsident beabsichtigt in der Tat, bei dem trilateralen Treffen mit Xi Jinping und Wladimir Putin über Iran zu sprechen«, sagte der US-Beamte, der anonym bleiben wollte, Journalisten in einer Telefonkonferenz. Hinsichtlich Kyjiw und Moskau verfolge Washington jedoch eine »völlig andere Verhandlungslinie«. »China ist nicht wirklich Teil dieser Verhandlungslinie, daher erscheint es nicht angebracht, die Ukrainefrage dort zu erörtern«, sagte der Regierungsvertreter.
Das Treffen von Trump, Putin und Xi in China war erwartet worden. Es weckte Befürchtungen, die Staatschefs könnten versuchen, die Einfluss-Sphären unter sich aufzuteilen.
Trump hat im Ukrainekrieg wiederholt prorussische Standpunkte vertreten und den ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj kritisiert. China stellt sich im Ukrainekrieg als neutral dar; Kiew und der Westen werfen China aber vor, Russlands Krieg entscheidend zu unterstützen.
Merz mit Botschaft für Trump
Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz hat US-Präsident Donald Trump vor dessen geplantem Treffen mit Kremlchef Wladimir Putin aufgerufen, mit den europäischen Verbündeten an der Seite der Ukraine zu stehen. Bei einem Treffen der Staats- und Regierungschefs der EU in Dublin »befürchten einige«, das für kommende Woche geplante Treffen zwischen Trump und Putin in China »könnte sozusagen ein zweiter Anchorage-Moment werden«, sagte Merz am Freitag in Dublin.
Trump hatte Putin im August 2025 mit Handschlag auf einem Militärflugplatz in Anchorage im Bundesstaat Alaska zu Gesprächen über den Ukrainekrieg empfangen. Zu Ehren des russischen Präsidenten ließ Trump sogar einen roten Teppich ausrollen. Kritiker warfen dem US-Präsidenten deswegen vor, dem wegen des russischen Angriffskriegs gegen die Ukraine vom Westen weitgehend geächteten Putin eine Bühne geboten zu haben.
»Ich will deswegen unsere Botschaft an die USA auch noch einmal sehr deutlich sagen: Bitte keine Überraschungen. Spielt weiter im Team Europa und im Team mit der Ukraine und lasst uns gemeinsam für einen echten Frieden in der Ukraine arbeiten«, hob der Bundeskanzler hervor. »Das ist unser Ziel, an dem halten wir fest.«
Nach neun Monaten Pause verhandeln Russland und die Ukraine wieder unter Vermittlung der USA. Moskau und Washington reden von einer neuen Sicherheitsarchitektur. Was ist realistisch?

A129.text:
Microsoft says all services working again
November 14, 2026
The US technology conglomerate Microsoft said on Saturday that a more than 24-hour global outage affecting its Microsoft 365 applications used by businesses and governments across the world has now ended.
"We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions," the company posted on X.
Microsoft applications such as Teams, Outlook and Copilot were all hit by the outage, leading to communications problems in scores of countries.
The company has said it was "not aware" of any outside interference that could have been behind the outage, blaming the problem on server issues.
The disruption was one of the longest in Microsoft's history and the second this year.
What effects did the Microsoft outage have?
The outage, which began around 1725 UTC on Thursday according to web testing and network diagnostics company Ookla, affected government agencies and businesses across much of the world.
It made it impossible to carry out activities such as sending emails and holding online meetings.
Germany was no exception, with a spokesperson for its Federal Ministry for Digital Transformation and Government Modernization saying that while the outage did not have a major impact on federal government functions, it did significantly affect German businesses.
Britain's state health service (NHS) was also severely affected, with personnel forced to have recourse to paper records rather than those stored online.
Altogether, there were more than 7.4 million reports of problems worldwide logged by Downdetector, which monitors online outages.
The disruption highlights the widespread and perilous reliance of governments and businesses on a very small number of Big Tech companies.
Tthe problems at Microsoft are so far believed to be unconnected with the major communications outage that has affected US aviation.

A138.text:
Beijing faces its Russia dilemma amid talk of Xi-Trump-Putin summit
November 13, 2026
An unprecedented meeting between the leaders of China, Russia and the United States could be happening on the sidelines of Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen next week.
China has yet to confirm that the meeting will take place. However, a Chinese Foreign Ministry official recently told the press that Beijing was "in communication" with relevant parties. In Moscow, a Kremlin representative said work on "coordination" was underway.
The clearest indication about the potential summit came from US President Donald Trump last weekend. Talking to reporters at a Florida airport, Trump said he "thinks" one of the meetings planned for APEC will be with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Is the world set for a 'new Yalta'?
Despite the lack of official confirmation from either Beijing, Moscow, or Washington, the media has already dubbed the potential trilateral summit a "new Yalta," invoking the optics of the US, UK, and Soviet Union convening at the end of World War II and deciding on the new geopolitical power balance in the Crimean resort town.
At the same time, nobody seems to be quite sure what the three leaders would talk about if China agrees to host the trilateral summit at APEC.
In his brief remarks to reporters on Sunday, Trump avoided mentioning Russia's war in Ukraine when asked about the possibility of the meeting, bringing up only "Iran" and "denuclearization" as possible talking points.
The Chinese Foreign Ministry reported "no information" when questioned earlier this week about the potential substance of talks.
End of campaign to isolate Putin?
A three-way meeting with a photo op would be a big diplomatic win for Russia's President Putin. Since launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Kremlin chief has faced years of diplomatic boycott by Kyiv's allies, most notably the US under Trump's predecessor Joe Biden.
Putin first pitched the idea of a trilateral summit last month during a call with Trump. The Wall Street Journal has reported that Putin wanted the meeting to discuss an end to his war in Ukraine.
For the US, the president standing shoulder to shoulder with the leaders of America's foremost rivals could be a bad look, although Trump has already made a show of personally greeting both leaders with a red carpet at different points during his second term.
As host, China is in an even trickier position. While Russia and China are broadly aligned on many issues, Beijing does not want to be explicitly tied to Russia's war in Ukraine and harm China's efforts to present itself as a long-term force for global stability.
EU wary of being left out of Ukraine talks
The Chinese government is also working to rebalance economic ties with the EU. The European powers would likely bristle at a summit hosted by China and discussing the war in Ukraine without Kyiv or Brussels present at the table.
"China is clearly uneasy about the possible trilateral meeting with the US and Russia, and although Beijing has shifted its position from saying nothing to admitting that the three powers are in contact, the vagueness of these declarations seems deliberate," Alicja Bachulska, Asia policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told DW.
"Beijing is aware of the potential negative optics of the 'Yalta 2.0' framing, even if this historical comparison is inaccurate and does not reflect current geopolitical dynamics," Bachulska said.
She notes the trilateral meeting could "trigger further escalation in the already worsening relations between China and the EU" if Ukraine is discussed with no Europeans in the room.
For China, there is also little to gain in terms of optics. Images of Xi standing with Trump, the leader of Beijing's top rival, and Putin, Beijing's partner in opposing the US, could present an awkward look.
[truncated]

Turkey and Qatar signed a mutual defence agreement Friday, pledging a unified response to any attack on either country, the two leaders said in a joint statement. The defence pact follows the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed by Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in August.
Turkey and Qatar signed a mutual defence agreement on Friday aimed at strengthening collective defence and promoting regional security, and pledged a unified stance against any external armed attack targeting either country, according to a joint statement issued after talks between their leaders.
The two sides agreed to consult on threats to their security, as well as regional and global security issues and defence policies, and to expand cooperation through joint military exercises, defence-industry cooperation and personnel training exchanges.

A192.text:
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday that four government agencies favoured putting Megaspeed, the Singapore company at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, on a trade black list, but not the Commerce Department that was in charge.
Bessent said Treasury, the Pentagon, the State Department and the U.S. Trade Representative’s Office had favoured adding Megaspeed to the Commerce Department entity list for months. “But Commerce has the pen,” Bessent told CNBC’s Squawk Box. “You will have to ask them about their internal processes.”
The Commerce Department’s so-called entity list is a trade blacklist of groups connected to China that U.S. officials say pose national security risks. The department did not immediately return a request for comment.
U.S. Senate Banking Committee chair calls on Huang, Lutnick to testify over Nvidia scandal
There is growing criticism of U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick’s role in overseeing export controls on U.S. chips to China. Lutnick reportedly stalled President Donald Trump’s crackdown on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia’s chips to China, media outlets reported this week.

Reuters reported Thursday that senior White House officials are discussing whether Lutnick should be pushed out amid a spy scandal surrounding Nvidia’s NVDA-Q now-former CEO Jensen Huang.
Bessent added that the administration was working to shut down “leakage” in the chip-export system and pointed to questions over how well Nvidia vetted its partner company amid CEO Jensen Huang’s exit this week, which sent shock waves across the AI industry.

A202.text:
Ukraine fired almost 1,200 drones at Russian targets overnight in one of its biggest aerial attacks since Moscow’s invasion nearly five years ago.
Meanwhile, U.S. and Russian negotiators raised the stakes in talks to stop the fighting by including for discussion wider European security arrangements that have been in place since the end of the Cold War. That change, long sought by Moscow, has alarmed European leaders and placed a question mark over NATO’s future role.
“Russia wants to talk about questions of European security architecture. We don’t need to talk about that. There is one,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, referring to the NATO military alliance.
After two days of talks with Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi this week, U.S. envoys went in person to brief Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was meeting with European leaders in Dublin, Ireland.
Further talks are planned as negotiators seek a breakthrough in peace efforts, according to U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.
Europe sees a Russian ‘trap’ in talks about continental security
Kushner said Russia has agreed to include Europe in upcoming talks, after Moscow’s long insistence that the continent’s governments should be excluded because they were part of the problem by supporting Ukraine.
Europe’s presence at the negotiating table will allow negotiators “to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia,” Kushner said on X.
As European leaders scrambled to find an envoy to the talks, they were also wary of Russian manoeuvring as well as Trump’s praise for Putin and his administration’s sharp criticism of Europe.
The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said Friday that Europe must insist on a ceasefire before taking the negotiations further – the opposite of what Putin demands.
Russia and Ukraine agree to large-scale prisoner swap as talks conclude with no major breakthrough
“If we start to talk about what Russia is asking regarding the security architecture, we actually walk into the traps that Russia is setting us,” she said in Dublin.
Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden insisted that Europe must take its fate into its own hands. “We cannot let neither the Americans nor the Russians decide about our future,” Frieden said.
Moscow is aiming “to dismantle NATO and the post-Cold War European security architecture,” the Institute for the Study of War said in an assessment late Thursday.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov reaffirmed that Russia is open for contacts with the Europeans.
“Once we understand [Europe’s] true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to make a decision on holding a dialogue regarding a settlement in Ukraine in an expanded format,” Peskov said.
Starlink problems again raise spectre of less U.S. support for Ukraine
Zelensky on Friday repeated his complaints about drone speed limits on the U.S. Starshield system – SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service – that Ukraine needs for its defence.
The speed restrictions are limiting Ukrainian drones to 161 kph on the entire front line and in Russian-occupied territory, he said, making it impossible for Ukraine to deploy its interceptors effectively against Russia’s fast-moving jet-powered drones.
“We still have no clear explanations,” he said of the unannounced restrictions, after first raising the issue on Thursday.
Starlink slowdown weakens Ukraine’s defences against Russia, Zelensky says
Ukrainian officials are asking the U.S. Department of State, the Pentagon and SpaceX to clarify and resolve the situation, he said.
Last month, similar SpaceX limits on Ukrainian drone speeds severely disrupted operations, alarming Kyiv officials who fear a drop in U.S. support.

A285.text:

Europe Agrees on a Team to Represent It in Talks With Russia
After coveting a seat in the Ukraine war discussions, Europe is poised to get one. The continent wants to fill it with a six-member team.
European leaders have waited on the margins of negotiations to end Russia’s war in Ukraine for months, eyeing a seat at the table. They learned this week that they would get one, and simply needed to decide which official should sit in that chair.
Instead, they decided on six.
European Union leaders concluded in Dublin on Friday that they will tap a group of major nations — Britain, France, Germany, Poland, and Italy — along with a representative from the E.U’s leadership arms, the European Council and European Commission.
In some ways, the choice of a crowd plays into jibes Americans have made about the continent’s indecisiveness: “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation,” Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and a U.S. envoy, said earlier this week.
Europe’s failure to pick one negotiator leaves open the possibility that its fragmentation will diminish its influence. Even so, Europeans have underscored that they are a democracy of many nations and that many voices must be represented.
“We decide on who represents us, and that is what we have done today,” said Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission.
“We need to work as a team,” António Costa, president of the European Union’s political leadership arm, said at a news conference on Friday, noting that America itself has two envoys.
