A294.text:
Lutnick Took a Softer Line on Nvidia as Calls for Tougher Controls Grew
Critics say Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, and his department have shielded Nvidia as concerns have grown over A.I. chip sales to firms like Megaspeed.
There is broad agreement among most senior Trump administration officials that the United States should more aggressively tighten controls on Nvidia’s advanced chips to keep China from using them to catch up in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
Then there is Howard Lutnick, who runs the Commerce Department.
Over the past year, Mr. Lutnick has frequently clashed with top officials over how to regulate sales of advanced technology, particularly Nvidia’s chip sales to Asia. That has drawn accusations from others in the administration and in Congress that the Commerce Department has become too cozy with Nvidia and its co-founder, Jensen Huang, and failed to adequately police the firm’s chip sales to China, in particular.
The issue has exploded into public view in recent weeks with the revelations from The New York Times that Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, was in a relationship with a woman believed by U.S. intelligence agencies to be a Chinese spy. The woman, Alice Huang, was a top executive at a Singapore-based company, Megaspeed, that is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. On Thursday, Mr. Huang announced that he was stepping down from the company, sending the company’s shares tumbling.
The astonishing developments have thrust Mr. Lutnick into an uncomfortable spotlight and raised questions about whether he went too far in protecting Nvidia’s interests. And it has focused attention on whether the influence of Mr. Huang, an ally of President Trump’s and among the most high-profile and successful of American business leaders, kept the United States from moving faster to clamp down on sales of Nvidia chips to companies like Megaspeed.
The stakes in the A.I. race between the United States and China are high. China hawks warn that allowing sales of advanced chips to that country is speeding its A.I. development and giving it an economic and military edge. Those who support the sales say they help U.S. technology maintain global leadership, while deterring China from developing rival products. As the head of a sprawling department that has control over enforcing restrictions on technology sales, Mr. Lutnick is best positioned to single-handedly shape whether China has access to American technology, including Nvidia’s.
Within the Commerce Department, Nvidia is treated differently than other firms, current and former officials say, with its issues given high priority and sent through specific channels.

A304.text:
AT A GLANCE
- Microsoft announced the restoration of services across Teams, Outlook, and other products after a global outage lasting over 24 hours, attributed to server issues rather than malicious activity.
- The outage significantly impacted businesses and government agencies worldwide, causing disruptions in essential functions like email communication and virtual meetings, with over 7.4 million outage reports logged.
- This incident raises concerns about the reliability of major tech companies and their services, as it marks the second major outage for Microsoft in 2023, prompting discussions about the risks of relying heavily on a single provider.
Microsoft said on Saturday, November 14, that services had fully recovered across Teams, Outlook and its other products, ending a global outage that crippled online communications for businesses and governments for over 24 hours.
“We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions,” the company posted on X.
Microsoft had said server issues were behind the incident that also affected its Copilot AI assistant, and that it was not aware of any malicious activity, ruling out AI as the cause.
Outlook and Teams are two of the most widely used workplace applications with hundreds of millions of users. The outage prevented people from performing essential functions such as sending emails, managing calendars and hosting virtual meetings.
It affected government agencies from Australia and Japan to the United States, caused delays at trading firms, hindered some companies from publishing earnings and prompted airlines to warn customers of communication lags, according to public statements.
Organizations that host Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than in the cloud, were somewhat spared.
Another outage for Microsoft
The outage, reports of which started climbing around 1725 GMT on Thursday according to Ookla, is one of the longest in Microsoft’s history and the second disruption to its services this year.
Microsoft said the outage specifically hit features tied to Exchange Online — its cloud-based email and scheduling hub — leaving unconnected applications operational.
The incident deepens questions about the global reliance on a handful of Big Tech companies that supply both the essential software and the cloud infrastructure that underpins it.
It also highlighted the dependence on Microsoft’s workplace software, with outage reports spiking as employees began their workdays across Asia and Europe, according to Downdetector’s parent company, Ookla.
Downdetector logged more than 7.4 million reports worldwide, peaking at nearly 20,000 a minute, more than 1,500 times normal levels.
“It shows how much of the working day now runs through one provider’s email and collaboration tools,” said Luke Kehoe, lead industry analyst at Ookla.
Microsoft shares closed flat at $523.88 on Friday. The stock has gained roughly 8% so far this year.
Disruptions and financial losses from the outage could result in numerous insurance claims, but the overall hit to insurers is expected to be limited, said Mario De Cicco, vice president of European financial institutions at Morningstar DBRS.
De Cicco estimated global insured losses from the incident at between $300 million and $500 million, well below the $400 million to $1.5 billion financial toll from the 2024 CrowdStrike outage that crashed more than 8 million Windows-based computers and caused widespread disruptions.
Microsoft also faced an outage with its 365 services in January this year and in October last year. Last month, it reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that impacted its suite of productivity software and a range of industries worldwide.
“The bigger worry is that this is not the first Microsoft 365 outage this year,” said Josh Gilbert, a market analyst at trading platform eToro.

A36.text:
Turkey, Qatar sign mutual defence agreement, pledge unified stance against attack
ISTANBUL, Nov 13 (Reuters) - Turkey and Qatar signed a mutual defence agreement on Friday aimed at strengthening collective defence and promoting regional security, and pledged a unified stance against any external armed attack targeting either country, according to a joint statement issued after talks between their leaders.
The two sides agreed to consult on threats to their security, as well as regional and global security issues and defence policies, and to expand cooperation through joint military exercises, defence-industry cooperation and personnel training exchanges.
Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan signed the accord during a meeting in Istanbul with Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani.
The agreement reflected the two countries' commitment to safeguarding their sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as their shared vision of a more secure and stable regional order, Turkey and Qatar said in the joint communique following the 12th session of their Supreme Strategic Committee.
"PresidentErdogan stated that we would continue working together to prevent the resurgence of war in the Gulf region and establish a basis for dialogue and achieve peace," the Turkish presidency said in a statement on X.
The countries also expressed readiness to pursue energy cooperation, particularly in liquefied natural gas trade, building on their long-standing relationship, the joint statement added.
The Turkish presidency had said Turkey and Qatar were working to develop and diversify their energy partnership and that their cooperation in the defence industry would continue to grow.
In August, Turkey,Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a jointdefence agreement in Mecca, bringing together the Sunni Muslim US allies at a time of conflict across the region.
Turkey's parliament ratified the so-called Mecca Joint Defence Agreement last week,clearing the way for Ankara to send military support to Saudi Arabia, which has been struggling to fend off attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants.
Under the agreement, signed by the three regional powers in August, an attack on one party constitutes an attack on all.
(Reporting by Daren Butler and Enas Alashray and Muhammad Al Gebaly in Cairo; Editing by Aidan Lewis and Ros Russell)

A449.text:
S’pore authorises first carbon credit project in Rwanda
ANTALYA, Turkey — Carbon-tax liable firms in Singapore could soon buy carbon credits from a water purification project in Rwanda to shrink their tax bill.
The National Environment Agency (NEA) said on Nov 14 that both countries have authorised the project by developer Climate Bridge International.
The project entails the distribution of 300,000 water filters that will provide access to safe drinking water without having to boil it using firewood or charcoal.
By reducing reliance on these fuels for water treatment, the project will also reduce emissions and indoor air pollution.
The filters will provide safe drinking water to about 1.8 million people, and save around 780,000 tonnes of emissions from 2026 to 2030. This is equivalent to taking about 184,000 cars off the road for a year.
Spending less time to collect firewood is also expected to give people more time for education, income-generating activities and community participation, said NEA.
This is the first project that has been authorised under Singapore’s carbon credit framework.
Under the framework, tax-liable companies here can buy eligible carbon credits to offset up to 5 per cent of their taxable emissions.
The credits can come only from authorised projects in countries that Singapore has implementation agreements with.
Rwanda is one of 12 countries that Singapore has such agreements with, and there are currently more than 20 projects undergoing assessment under the Singapore-Rwanda implementation agreement.
An implementation agreement is a legally binding document that governs the international transfer of carbon credits between two countries.
A key element of these agreements is to prevent double counting, which is where both the buyer and host country count the same emissions reductions or removals towards their own targets.
A host country must agree to make a “corresponding adjustment” to add the sold emissions back to its national inventory.
Of the 12 implementation agreements, six have been operationalised, which means that the applications for projects have been called.
The six countries are: Ghana, Bhutan, Peru, Rwanda, Thailand and Mongolia.
NEA made the announcement about the first authorisation from Rwanda alongside the ongoing UN climate summit COP31, which is being held in the Turkish city of Antalya.
Representatives from nearly 200 countries are gathered there to discuss how to tackle climate change.
One way to do this is through the carbon markets.
Under the Paris Agreement, which aims to limit global warming to 1.5 deg C above pre-industrial levels, countries can buy credits generated elsewhere as long as the climate benefit is not double counted by host and buyer countries.
One carbon credit represents one tonne of carbon dioxide that is either prevented from being released – by saving a forest from the axe, for example – or removed from the atmosphere, such as from a direct air capture plant.
The carbon markets contribute to climate action, as it directs funds from carbon emitters to developing countries hosting these green projects.
Under the Rwanda project, 300,000 ceramic water filters will be distributed to households and early childhood development centres across Rwanda, largely in the Western Province.
The project will support Rwanda’s national climate targets, which include improving access to safe drinking water.
An initial number of 10,000 water filters has been distributed in June 2026 with the remaining to be progressively deployed in 2027, said NEA.
The implementation agreement between Singapore and Rwanda has three stages.
At each stage, both countries assess applications against their own requirements.
For Singapore, projects must meet Singapore’s eligibility criteria, for high-integrity carbon credits, where the climate benefit can be trusted and verified.
At the second stage, both countries will issue letters of authorisation to approved projects.

A450.text:
China, US discuss tariffs, farm trade ahead of Xi-Trump meeting
- China and the US held their first trade council meeting on 13 November. They discussed tariff cuts, farm trade and other issues before a Xi-Trump meeting in Shenzhen.
- China said talks were “candid, in-depth and constructive”, but gave no sign of any deal. Both sides will keep using the council to ease trade tensions and solve disputes.
- A proposed US$60 billion tariff-cut plan is still not finalised. China says Washington must implement it first, while US farm imports from China may stay weak despite buy pledges.
AI generated
BEIJING – China and the United States discussed tariff cuts, agricultural trade and other issues at their first trade council meeting on Nov 13, China’s Commerce Ministry said on Nov 14, days ahead of an expected leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen later in November.
“The two sides held candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges on implementing the outcomes of previous China-US economic and trade talks, including tariffs, a reciprocal ‘US$30 billion (S$38.6 billion)-for-US$30 billion’ tariff-cut arrangement, agricultural trade and other issues of mutual concern,” the ministry said.
It did not say whether any agreements were reached.
Both sides will continue using the council to address trade concerns, expand cooperation and reduce outstanding issues, the ministry added.
Following a September summit between Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump in Washington, the two sides proposed a US$60 billion package of reciprocal tariff cuts, including roughly US$17 billion worth of US farm goods that China imported in 2024, but the plan has yet to be finalised.
Chinese purchases of US farm goods other than soybeans are on track to hit a seven-year low in 2026, despite an agreement to buy US$17 billion annually through 2028, a Reuters analysis of customs data showed earlier in November, underscoring persistent uncertainty over the deal.
Beijing has repeatedly urged Washington to implement the US$60 billion tariff-reduction deal, calling it a prerequisite for increasing purchases of US farm goods.
The White House said Trump will meet Xi on Nov 19 on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen. REUTERS

A458.text:
Trump to raise nuclear-arms cuts with Putin, Xi on Nov 19, White House says
- Trump will raise nuclear arms cuts with Putin and Xi at a China meeting on Nov 19, the White House said, calling nuclear spread “very dangerous”.
- China has rejected talks on nuclear arms with the US and Russia, saying they should speak directly because they have the biggest stockpiles.
- No deal is expected, but the White House says the talks could start a useful future conversation; Trump will also discuss Iran, not Ukraine.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump will raise nuclear-arms reduction at a meeting in China next week with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, the White House said on Nov 13.
“He will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, said on a call with reporters. She added that the meeting would take place on Nov 19 in China.
Trump’s repeated insistence that the first-of-its-kind meeting of the three leaders focus on nuclear arms reductions has riled China, which is hosting a summit focused on trade and commerce. China has rebuffed attempts to talk about nuclear arms with Russia and the United States, which have the largest stockpiles of such weapons.
Putin, Xi and Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen. Trump is leaving on Nov 16 for a four-day trip to Asia that also includes a stop in the Philippines.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior Trump administration official said regarding the nuclear issue. “This is a difficult topic for China to address, but we do think it’s time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults’ table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things.”
The official added: “This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”
Beijing has for years resisted direct engagement with Washington about its nuclear programme, saying it is more appropriate for Russia and the US to speak directly because of their large arsenals.
Russia has the most stored nuclear warheads, followed by the United States and China, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty between the US and Russia expired in 2026.
It was not clear whether Russia or China intended to engage in a conversation about arms reductions with Trump.
The Chinese and Russian embassies in Washington did not immediately respond to e-mailed requests for comment.
Trump will also raise the US-Israeli war against Iran in the meeting but is not expected to raise Russia’s war in Ukraine, the official said.
The Republican president is not expected to have a one-on-one meeting with Putin or discuss Ukraine’s access to satellite communications service provided by Elon Musk’s SpaceX. Musk is joining Trump on the trip to China but will not attend his meeting with Xi and Putin, according to the official.
“We’ve had many meetings recently with the Russians, but China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” the person said.
Trump is also not expected to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his trip to Asia, according to the official. REUTERS

A465.text:
Inside Microsoft’s rush to get back online after a global outage
Karen Weise
- Microsoft engineers worked through the night after a global outage hit Outlook, Teams and Copilot, disrupting hospitals, schools, businesses and offices.
- Microsoft said a recent network upgrade caused some servers to fail, and it restored services slowly to avoid overload and keep systems stable.
- The outage may have manageable financial costs, but analysts said it could damage Microsoft’s reputation and push customers to rethink their dependence on its cloud services.
AI generated
Late into the night on Nov 12, hundreds of Microsoft engineers and top executives were sitting in their darkened offices or home basements, logged in to a videoconference triaging a nightmare scenario for a technology company.
The world still runs on email, and much of that is processed through Microsoft Outlook. For hours, a company outage affected hospitals, schools, businesses and congressional offices in Washington. Even Microsoft’s own staff couldn’t use email.
On the videoconference, Scott Guthrie, the senior executive overseeing the company’s computing infrastructure, was proposing possible fixes, according to a person familiar with the call who was not authorised to speak publicly. People chewed on fingernails, rubbed their foreheads and debated how to turn off other services to prevent a “stampeding herd” so that as systems come back online, they would not be overwhelmed with new demands and shut back down.
By the morning of Nov 13, the company had apologised at least twice. It said it determined that the problem stemmed from a recent upgrade to its network, which shut down some servers, and that the systems were steadily improving. “Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage,” the company said in a statement. “While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.”
Finally, they had kept the herd at bay.
The prolonged and widespread outage was just the most recent reminder that the technological underpinnings of modern life and business are run through just a handful of major companies. And while cyberattacks and malicious actors can target their systems, sometimes the companies learn the hard way that they can introduce devastating flaws when updating or maintaining their own global systems.
For Microsoft, the problems from this week’s outage are not done yet. The short-term financial fallout should be “manageable,” analysts at investment bank William Blair wrote in a research note on Nov 13. But they said this prolonged outage is a reputational hit that could make companies and other customers reconsider having so much riding on one technology provider.
“We believe the outage could prompt enterprises to reassess their dependence on Microsoft’s infrastructure,” they wrote.
Outlook and other services affected, including Teams and its artificial intelligence assistant Copilot, are part of Microsoft 365’s cloud subscription business, which is used by more than 450 million people and brought in almost US$28 billion (S$36 billion) in its last quarter, which ended Sept 30. NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

A466.text:
Bessent blames US Commerce Dept over lack of export controls for Nvidia partner Megaspeed
- Scott Bessent said Treasury, Defence, State and the US Trade Representative backed blacklisting Megaspeed, but the Commerce Department did not act because “Commerce has the pen”.
- Critics say Commerce Secretary Lutnick stalled export controls on Nvidia chips to China. Senators John Curtis and Richard Blumenthal attacked his role and called for tougher action.
- The scandal has raised fears of weak checks at Nvidia and possible chip leakage to China. Bessent said the government has enough powers and must use them.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Nov 13 that four government agencies had favoured putting Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company at the heart of the Nvidia scandal, on a trade blacklist but not the Commerce Department that was in charge.
Bessent said the Treasury, the Pentagon, the State Department and the US Trade Representative’s Office had favoured adding Megaspeed to the Commerce Department entity list for months.
“But Commerce has the pen,” Bessent told CNBC’s Squawk Box. “You will have to ask them about their internal processes.”
The Commerce Department’s so-called entity list is a trade blacklist of groups connected to China that US officials say pose national security risks. The department did not immediately return a request for comment.
There is growing criticism of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s role in overseeing export controls on US chips to China.
Lutnick reportedly stalled President Donald Trump’s crackdown on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia’s chips to China, media outlets reported this week.
Republican Senator John Curtis said on Nov 13 that “Secretary Lutnick’s reported stalling on export controls raises the question of whether the Commerce Department is acting in the best interests of the American people”.
Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal said on Nov 13 that “Lutnick must go”.
“His malign self-enriching malfeasance shows the costs of corruption – putting personal profit above public interest.
“Making powerful Nvidia chips available to China through an apparent spy undercut both national security and economic competitiveness.”
Megaspeed has been in the spotlight following reports that Jensen Huang had an affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect of being a Chinese spy.
Reuters reported on Nov 12 that senior White House officials are discussing whether Lutnick should be pushed out amid a spy scandal surrounding Nvidia’s now-former CEO Huang.
Bessent added that the administration was working to shut down “leakage” in the chip export system, and pointed to questions over how well Nvidia vetted its partner company amid CEO Huang’s exit this week, which had sent shock waves across the artificial intelligence industry.
US lawmakers have called for tougher restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips in the wake of the scandal, which has threatened to implicate some Trump administration members, including Lutnick, amid growing questions over the administration’s oversight of chip sales to China.
“The real story here should be, did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?” Bessent said.
“It’s important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that.”
Asked if Congress needed to step in to act on export controls, he said: “We have all the authorities that we need. They just need to be implemented.”
Senate Banking Committee chairman Tim Scott on Nov 12 asked Lutnick to testify. REUTERS

A477.text:
Zelenskiy says restrictions still in place on Starshield, hampering operations inside Ukraine
Nov 13 - President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Friday that speed restrictions remained in place on the US Starshield satellite communications system, hampering the Ukrainian military's ability to operate inside the country.
Zelenskiy said the continued restrictions made it hard to intercept jet-powered and other drones and sent a bad signal to Russia on dealing with land seized by Russian forces in the 4 1/2-year war.
"Unfortunately, the speed restrictions remain in place along the entire front line and in temporarily-occupied territories of Ukraine," he said in his nightly video address.
"I expect the Ministry of Defence and the Foreign Ministry, together with all relevant structures in the United States, will work through this issue."
In mid-October, Ukrainian officials said Elon Musk's SpaceX had abruptly capped the speed of Starlink and its Starshield military version, cutting off drones and other equipment moving faster than about 160 kph (100 mph) amid tensions with the Trump administration over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Service was restored on October 24 and neither Musk nor the US government, which operates Starshield using Starlink technology, took responsibility for imposing the curbs.
On Thursday, Zelenskiy said Ukrainian military units had again recorded disruptions to Starshield over several days.
In his latest comments, Zelenskiy repeated that the restrictions "limit our ability to intercept jet-powered Shaheds (Iranian-designed drones) and counter other drones".
"They also send Russia a signal that America may somehow treat our temporarily-occupied land differently," he said. "We expect the speed to be restored." REUTERS

A491.text:
EU settles on five-nation group to speak for Europe at Ukraine peace talks
DUBLIN – European Union leaders have agreed that Europe’s team for Ukraine peace talks will comprise five major military powers – non-member Britain plus France, Germany, Italy and Poland – and EU institutions, European Council president Antonio Costa has said, after months of wavering over who will speak for the continent.
“Europe must speak with one clear voice and united voice in all discussions that shape the future of Ukraine and the security of our continent. And this is ultimately a team effort,” Costa, who chairs EU summits, told a press conference at the end of a leaders’ meeting in Dublin on Nov 13.
The Kremlin said on Nov 13 that Russia would be open to European countries taking part in Ukraine peace talks if it saw they genuinely intended to contribute to peace. Russian officials have also called for a broad agreement on Europe’s security architecture to be reached before specifics of the war are addressed.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz described the Kremlin’s comments as “the same old game” and said that Europe and the US had agreed on a clear message.
“There will be no discussions about Ukraine without Ukraine, and no discussions about Europe without Europe. Furthermore, there is no need to talk about European security architecture. We have that already,” Merz told reporters midway through the summit.
Kushner says US has begun talks on Europe’s security
US negotiator Jared Kushner said in Moscow on Nov 12 that he had begun discussions with European partners on the continent’s security architecture.
Representatives from Britain, France, Germany, Italy and the EU attended Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi this week, where both Moscow and Kyiv cited some progress, though there was no sign of a breakthrough on key issues such as territory.
EU officials said the representatives for Europe in future talks were likely to be national security advisers from the five military powers, plus delegates from the European Commission and the European Council, the body for EU governments. NATO is also expected to be represented.
Before its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russia demanded the withdrawal of NATO forces from countries that joined the alliance after 1997. NATO rejected the demand.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Russian calls for discussions about Europe’s security architecture threatened to divert attention from the need for a ceasefire. Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs called such discussions “a trap”.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it was important to avoid unnecessary concessions to Russia. “My view was shared by many others: There can be no revision of Europe’s security architecture – that is what Putin is demanding,” he said.
During a meeting on Nov 12, leaders from Poland, the Baltics and Nordic states warned against brainstorming with the US or Russia about Europe’s security architecture, according to a European diplomat and a European official.
Forty European countries, meeting as a broader group in Dublin on Nov 12, signed a declaration saying that any matter affecting European security should be decided with the involvement of Europeans. REUTERS

A493.text:
Turkey, Qatar sign mutual defence agreement, Turkish presidency says
ISTANBUL – Turkey and Qatar announced they have signed a mutual defence agreement, which they said was aimed at adopting a “unified position” in the face of an external attack.
The announcement on Nov 13 came after Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan met Qatari Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani in Istanbul.
Erdogan had said the agreement would further strengthen ties between the regional allies, according to his office.
Qatar’s ruler travelled to Istanbul after attending the United Nations COP31 climate summit in southern Turkey.
“The two parties hailed the signing of the mutual defence agreement between Qatar and Turkey,” according to a joint statement carried by Qatar’s state news agency.
The agreement was “aimed at bolstering collective defence and achieving regional security and stability, as well as adopting a unified position in the face of any external armed attack targeting either or both parties”, the statement said.
“The two parties agreed to hold consultations on threats to their security... and to strengthen cooperation through joint military exercises, collaboration in the field of defence industries, and the exchange of personnel training.”
Erdogan’s office had earlier announced the agreement, without going into the details of its contents.
“A mutual defence agreement signed by Turkey and Qatar today will add a new dimension to the brotherly ties between the two countries,” the Turkish President said during the meeting, according to the statement from his office.
He also said Turkey and Qatar would expand cooperation in the defence industry.
Iran war backdrop
In August, Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed a regional defence pact under which the three countries would come to one another’s aid if one of them came under attack.
Ratified by the Turkish Parliament last week, the pact links NATO member Turkey, which has the alliance’s second-largest military, with Pakistan, the Muslim world’s only nuclear-armed state, and Saudi Arabia, the Gulf’s leading power.
Turkey has said the agreement is not aimed at any other country and remains open to other states, including Egypt.
In October, Qatar, Indonesia, Pakistan and Turkey signed a multilateral memorandum of understanding on defence cooperation in Doha.
The agreement, known as “Badr”, aims to bolster cooperation between the participating countries.
Erdogan and the Qatari Emir also discussed the Iran war.
Turkey and Qatar would continue working together “to prevent a renewed outbreak of war in the Gulf region and to promote dialogue and peace”, Erdogan said.
The leaders discussed Israel’s attacks on Gaza and the humanitarian situation in the Palestinian territory, efforts towards normalisation in Syria and the latest developments in Libya, the statement added. AFP

A497.text:
Zelensky says no 'clear' reason given for new Starshield curbs
- Zelensky said Ukraine still has no “clear explanations” for new Starshield curbs, which he said affect the whole front line and Russian-occupied areas.
- Ukraine relies on SpaceX’s network for frontline communication and drones, but the limits may stop it intercepting Russian jet-drones that can reach 1,000 km/h.
- Zelensky ordered talks with the US State Department, the Pentagon and SpaceX to resolve the issue; Ukraine first reported Starshield problems in October after a row with Donald Trump.
AI generated
KYIV – Ukraine is yet to receive an explanation for why access to the Starshield satellite communications network has been restricted, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Nov 13.
Kyiv relies on the network for its frontline communications and operating drones, including interceptors that shoot down incoming Russian drones.
Zelensky said on Nov 12 that Ukraine’s military was facing “systematic” restrictions on the service, operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, with connections only working when devices were moving slower than 161kmh.
“We still have no clear explanations,” Zelensky said on Nov 13, confirming the restrictions were still in place “along the entire front line” and over territory occupied by Russia.
“I instructed Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Minister of Defense to step up contacts with the US Department of State, the Pentagon, and SpaceX to obtain clarification and resolve the situation,” he said on social media.
A source in the defence ministry said the speed limit did not apply in areas controlled by Ukraine.
Kyiv says the restrictions effectively make it impossible for them to intercept Russia’s jet-drones, which can travel at up to 1,000 km/h.
Ukraine first reported problems using Starshield in October following a row between Zelensky and US President Donald Trump over a US-Russia diesel deal, before access was eventually restored. AFP

A498.text:
Ukraine races to repair power plants wrecked by Russian missiles before winter
Nov 13 - Oleksiy, a technician at a Ukrainian power plant, has lost count of how many times he has had to repair the facility after Russian attacks. But the latest strike was the most devastating, he says, and could leave an entire region without heat and electricity this winter.
Early one morning this month, Russian missiles slammed into the plant — owned by Ukraine's largest private energy company, DTEK — tearing apart its roof and walls. Turbines and boilers were buried under tons of debris that hundreds of workers must clear by hand.
Reuters visited the ruined plant but DTEK asked not to disclose its location for security reasons.
"Right now, everyone has shovels and wheelbarrows as we try to reach the equipment," said Oleksiy, who asked to be identified only by his given name. "The main thing is to get to it, assess its condition and only then make plans for repairs and restoration."
Russia resumed large-scale attacks on energy infrastructure in mid-autumn, seeking to weaponise Ukraine's harsh winters by leaving millions without heat and electricity, as it has sought to do every year since its full-scale invasion in 2022. Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians.
But this year, Ukraine has struggled to protect its power plants after the US cut deliveries of Patriot interceptors — the only weapon in Kyiv's arsenal capable of stopping Russian ballistic missiles — amid a global shortage.
Ukraine's defences have also been stretched by Russia's deployment of new jet-powered attack drones, which are more difficult to down because of their speed.
Last winter, the coldest of the war, DTEK's five plants came under heavy attack 11 times. But already this November, the first month of the current heating season, Russia has attacked three of DTEK's plants with dozens of missiles and drones, forcing the stations to halt electricity generation.
"They (the Russians) seem obsessed with leaving us without electricity and heating, and they stick to that goal," said Oleksiy. "But we restore what they destroy and keep working."
DTEK workers have restarted its plants from scratch more than 70 times during the war following Russian attacks.
But analysts say this winter could be more difficult because of the more destructive attacks. Many Ukrainian cities, including Kyiv, are already experiencing long blackouts.
"It's difficult to say how quickly we can recover," DTEK CEO Maxim Timchenko told Reuters. "So we do everything possible to make enough power generation capacity in Ukraine to get through the winter."
'YOU'RE A TARGET'
By the light of lamps powered by portable generators, workers break chunks of concrete and cut pipes to reach equipment still buried beneath the rubble.
"It reduces me to tears. I know what it looked like when it was intact — everything was lit up, painted and working, producing electricity," said Mykhailo, 46, a senior power-unit operator.
Clearing the rubble is complicated by constant air-raid alerts, during which workers must descend into Soviet-era underground shelters built to protect against possible NATO missiles.
An air-raid alarm sounded during the Reuters visit and reporters rushed to the cramped rooms beneath the facility. Dozens of people waited for the alert to end, alongside several dogs which, workers say, also seek refuge there.
"It's hard to live through all this when you know the missiles are coming specifically for you, that you are a target," said Mykhailo.
"Then you come home and feel grateful that you made it, that you are home again, that you can see your family — it's a mixture of fear and relief."
TRANSMISSION LINES TARGETED
Before the war, Ukraine's thermal power plants generated more than 30% of its electricity. However, their share has fallen sharply after repeated attacks and Ukraine's three nuclear power plants now account for the lion's share of output.

A522.text:
Tackling the climate crisis is central to all of human life and must be at the forefront of global governance, the outgoing UN secretary general has said in an emotional farewell address at the Cop31 climate summit.
“You cannot build peace on a burning planet,” António Guterres said at his final climate press conference as secretary general on Friday. “You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it. You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends.”
Guterres has been the most forthright secretary general yet on the subject of the climate, returning to it again and again to castigate fossil fuel companies and recalcitrant governments.
He leaves office at the end of December and his successor is still unknown after Donald Trump tried to interject his preferred choices into the process. There are widespread fears that the next incumbent will downplay the climate crisis in favour of other issues.
In a clear message to his successor, Guterres spelled out why the UN must continue to place the climate at the top of the global agenda. “Climate change does not stay in its lane,” he said. “It drives anger and displacement around the world. It wipes out development gains built over decades. It pushes countries deeper into deficit. It aggravates competition for land and water.
“It fuels instability. And increasingly, it threatens the very existence of communities and countries. For all these reasons, I have never viewed climate action as just one of many other issues. Climate action is central to every aspect of the work of the UN.”
Guterres was one of the few world leaders left at Cop by Friday afternoon as most of the more than 90 who had attended returned to their capitals, leaving negotiators to get down to tackling issues such as the electrification of the global economy and a just transition out of fossil fuel industries for workers.
The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, flew out after hosting a meeting between major international investors and Australian renewable energy companies, followed by a meeting with Taneti Maamau, the president of the low-lying Pacific nation of Kiribati. Albanese made raising the plight of his country’s Pacific neighbours a major part of his two and a half-days at the talks.
The Australian co-presidency of the 31st “conference of the parties” to the UN framework convention on climate change issued a list of “reflections” that encapsulated the proposals countries had expressed since the talks began on Monday. This will form a loose basis for a first draft of the “cover decision”, the final negotiated document gavelled through at the end of the summit, which is likely to be the central outcome of Cop31.
Recent cover decisions have produced significant progress: at Cop28, in Dubai in 2023, the cover decision included a global pledge to “transition away from fossil fuels”, and at Cop26, in Glasgow in 2021, a cover decision produced a requirement to “phase down” coal.
This year, hoped-for resolutions include a target of deriving 35% of final energy worldwide from electricity by 2035, seen as one of the most important ways of decarbonising the global economy, and pledges to cut methane emissions, make progress on the phase-out of fossil fuels, and ensure adequate finance for developing countries hit by climate disaster.
The “reflections” document gave a clear sense of how difficult it will be for Australia – which, in an unusual sharing arrangement, is presiding over the negotiations while Turkey hosts the talks – to forge an agreement before the scheduled end next Friday night.
Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister and the president of the negotiations, said: “We are making sure parties are being listened to as we progress negotiations. The reflection text is not a negotiating text.

A550.text:
- Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said speed restrictions remain in place on the US Starshield satellite communications system, hampering the Ukrainian military’s ability to operate inside the country. The continued restrictions made it hard to intercept jet-powered and other drones and sent a bad signal to Russia on dealing with land seized by Russian forces in the war, the Ukrainian president also said on Friday. “Unfortunately, the speed restrictions remain in place along the entire front line and in temporarily-occupied territories of Ukraine,” he said in his nightly video address. “I expect the ministry of defence and the foreign ministry, together with all relevant structures in the United States, will work through this issue.” Ukrainian officials said in mid-October that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had abruptly capped the speed of Starlink and its Starshield military version amid tensions with the US over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. Service was restored on 24 October.
- Zelenskyy said on Thursday Ukrainian military units had recorded disruptions to Starshield over several days. He repeated that the restrictions “limit our ability to intercept jet-powered Shaheds [Iranian-designed drones] and counter other drones”. “They also send Russia a signal that America may somehow treat our temporarily-occupied land differently,” he said. “We expect the speed to be restored.”
- Russia attacked a hospital in the centre of Kyiv, close to several western embassies, after Zelenskyy’s comments on the throttling of Starshield . Three people were injured when a drone smashed into the National Institute of Traumatology and Orthopedics at 3am, hitting the second floor of the hospital and an adjoining 19th-century building in the capital, reports Luke Harding. Meanwhile, Russia claimed to have shot down nearly 1,200 Ukrainian drones overnight, one of the largest swarms sent by Kyiv. It said at least four people were killed in the southern region of Volgograd.
- The EU’s foreign policy chief warned against “walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as she said Moscow was trying to start a debate about European security in order to divert attention from its aggression, reports Jennifer Rankin. “We have one aggressor and one victim, and the aggressor does not have security concerns,” Kaja Kallas said on arrival at an EU leaders’ summit in Dublin. In talks on the Ukraine war, Russia has revived its hardline demands for a total overhaul of European security – demands that were rejected in 2021.
- Russia has been rocked by two car bomb attacks that killed a senior military figure and seriously injured a suspected intelligence agent, in the latest in a series of assassination attempts believed to have been orchestrated by Kyiv. On Friday morning a car bomb exploded in southern Moscow, severely injuring Sergei Zavorotniy, 72, a former senior aide to Ukraine’s exiled former prime minister Mykola Azarov, reports Pjotr Sauer. The blast came a day after a car bomb explosion in St Petersburg killed a senior Russian military official. The official has not been publicly identified but a local broadcaster cited sources as saying the victim was a colonel in the Russian air force.
- Russian forces launched strikes on two Ukrainian cities on Friday, killing one person and injuring more than 50 in the south-eastern city of Zaporizhzhia and killing two more in the Black Sea port of Odesa, regional officials said. In Zaporizhzhia, a five-storey apartment building was hit and seriously damaged. A rescue worker was killed when a concrete slab collapsed during operations to clear rubble, regional governor Mykhailo Semikin said. In Odesa, two people died in an attack on a private residence, said the city’s military administration hed, Serhiy Lysak. Five people were injured.
- A general in Ukraine’s SBU security service suspected in a serious corruption case was released from pre-trial detention on Friday after posting $1.2m bail.

A555.text:
More than 100 corporations and industry groups linked to fossil fuel interests have sent delegations to the UN climate talks in Turkey, according to an analysis.
The Cop31 climate summit in Antalya is thought to be the largest ever in the three decades of the annual gatherings, with more than 92,000 delegates registered to attend talks aimed at shifting the world away from the fossil fuels that are dangerously overheating our planet.
This swell of people includes numerous groups that support or are influenced by coal, oil and gas interests, the review has found. In total, 103 groups with a track record of obstructing climate action or furthering fossil fuel interests are at Cop31, according to the Kick Big Polluters Out coalition, which comprises about 450 environmental organisations.
The groups include 60 fossil fuel industry bodies, 16 financial companies that fund fossil fuels, six industrial agriculture and foods products groups, three big tech groups and 20 cross-sector organisations.
Among the largest delegations are the International Emissions Trading Association, which has 29 people at Cop and has been accused of helping provide legitimacy to fossil fuel companies, BNP Paribas, HSBC and Amazon. The oil firm Exxon has a delegation of 13 people in Antalya, TotalEnergies has five and BlackRock, another big financier of fossil fuel projects, has five.
These delegations outnumber the national delegations sent by some of the countries most vulnerable to climate impacts. Nepal, which suffered a devastating, deadly glacier collapse this summer that has been linked to global heating, has just a sixth of the number of delegates of these groups.
Prakash Dahal from Pro Public/Friends of the Earth Nepal said: “Big polluters have caused loss of livelihood, emotional damage, trauma and survival challenges for our people.
“We cannot tolerate the disproportionate space given to them compared to civil society and our country delegations.”
Large numbers of fossil fuel lobbyists have long been a feature of the UN climate talks, with one in every 25 participants at last year’s summit in Brazil a fossil fuel lobbyist. Environmental advocates have called for better transparency and conflict of interest disclosures for those attending, and influencing, the climate talks.
Sheldon Whitehouse, a US senator and prominent climate advocate who is at Cop31, said: “The ticket to entry to this badge should be a disclosure form in which you lay out exactly who you funded in the climate space with how much, when.
“I think it’s important to know who the infiltrators are, who the moles are in the climate conversation and who are the legitimate participants. If people want to come they’ve got to come clean about their bad behaviour and they can’t hide it out in the real world and then come here and act like they’re responsible.”
TotalEnergies directed the Guardian to a statement on their website which says: “TotalEnergies aims to be a major player in the energy transition. Since 2020, TotalEnergies has been firmly committed to its transition strategy and TotalEnergies is currently the integrated energy major investing the most in the energy transition.” That is why the company attends Cop Conferences. “TotalEnergies is well on track to achieve its ambitious greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets, particularly regarding methane emissions. In this respect, TotalEnergies can and wishes to help drive progress across the industry.”
Unlike previous years when the Kick Big Polluters Out group counted the overall number of fossil fuel-aligned delegates, this time the organisation highlighted the companies and associations it says have slowed or blocked action on the climate crisis.
Large banks, for example, continue to provide major financial support for coal, oil and gas projects, and 30 banks with delegations at Cop31 account for more than $2.2tn (£1.6tn) in fossil fuel financing over the past five years.

A56.text:
Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
- Published
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.
The historic meeting between the respective leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.
It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Moscow and Beijing have yet to comment.
No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior US official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.
Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.
"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.
She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".
A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation that helped resolve the Cold War.
The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement that included China, which has been building up its arsenal.
Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could create major hurdles and take years.
Xi separately hosted both Putin and Trump in Beijing just days apart earlier this year, while the US president welcomed his Chinese counterpart to Washington in September.
Beijing has become a crucial trading partner for Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which has isolated Russia and left it subject to Western sanctions.
But a controversial US deal to import Russian diesel and the suspension of sanctions targeting the biggest buyers of Moscow's oil and gas - including China - heightened European concern about the Trump administration's softening towards the Kremlin last month.
Trump and Xi have meanwhile sought to project warmer ties at summits in Beijing and Washington this year - though little significant progress appeared to have been made on key issues such as trade, their race for AI dominance, and Taiwan.
The war in Iran has also been a sticking point, with Beijing the largest buyer of Tehran's oil and its largest trade partner.
Chinese state media reported on Friday that Xi would take part in "bilateral" talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, citing a foreign ministry spokesman, but has not reported on the trilateral meeting.
Earlier this month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media that there were "signals confirming readiness" for such talks at the summit.
